text: Mechanism of polysulfide dissolution suppression in Lithium-sulfur batteries using a novel fluorinated ether electrolyte Daisuke Okuda a, Minako Deguchi c , Shigeaki Yamazaki b , Masashi Ishikawa c,* a Organization for Research and Development of Innovative Science and Technology, Kansai University, 3-3-35 Yamate-cho, Suita, 564-8680, Japan b Product R&D Department Chemicals Division, Daikin Industries, Ltd., 1-1 Nishi-Hitotsuya, Settu, 566-8585, Japan c Department of Chemistry and Materials Engineering, Faculty of Chemistry, Materials and Bioengineering Kansai University, 3-3-35 Yamate-cho, Suita, 564-8680, Japan A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Lithium-sulfur batteries Fluoroether electrolyte Polysulfide ionization COSMO-RS analysis S K-edge XANES A B S T R A C T Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries are a promising high-energy-density storage technology, yet their practical application is hindered by the dissolution of lithium polysulfides (Li2Sx, 1 ≤x ≤8) and the resulting shuttle effect.
In this study, we demonstrate a novel electrolyte solvent, 1,1,1-trifluoro-2- (2-methoxyethoxy)ethane (C14), designed to suppress Li2Sx dissolution through steric and electronic modulation.

Electrochemical mea­ surements revealed that the Li-S cell using the C14-based electrolyte operated reversibly without the infinite charging plateau characteristic of the shuttle effect, which was observed in a conventional 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME)-based system.

Mechanistic investigations combining FT-IR, Raman spectroscopy, and COSMO-RS calcu­ lations indicated that the electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl group in C14 causes a delocalization of the molecular surface charge and restricts the conformational flexibility required for Li+ chelation.

Crucially, S Kedge X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure (XANES) analysis provided direct evidence of the solvation mech­ anism: while the DME system exhibited a pre-edge feature at 2470.3 eV attributed to Li defects generated by Li2Sx ionization, this feature was notably absent in the C14 system.
These results confirm that C14 effectively prevents the ionization and subsequent leaching of Li2Sx into the electrolyte.
This work establishes that suppressing solvent-induced ionization via charge delocalization is a vital strategy for realizing stable, high-performance Li-S batteries. 1.
Introduction Recent research has focused on developing high-energy-density storage devices to meet the growing demands of lightweight applica­ tions.
Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries are considered a promising tech­ nology due to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density [1].
A typical Li-S battery employs sulfur as the cathode and lithium metal as the anode.

During the charge-discharge process, the global electro­ chemical reactions are represented as follows [2]: S8 + 16Li+ + 16e−⇄8Li2S(1)Li⇄Li+ + en− (2) In reaction (1), sulfur undergoes a 16-electron redox process, yielding a high theoretical specific capacity of 1672 mAh g−1.
However, the practical application of sulfur is hindered by its inherent insulating nature, characterized by low electronic and ionic conductivities.
Extensive research has been conducted to enhance the conductivity of sulfur cathodes [3–7].
For instance, Ji et al. reported that a carbon-sulfur composite cathode, featuring sulfur encapsulated within a mesoporous carbon framework, exhibited a high specific capacity of 1200 mAh g−1 [3].
Despite these advances, the dissolution of intermediate lithium pol­ ysulfides (Li2Sx, 1 ≤x ≤8) into the electrolyte remains a critical chal­ lenge.
The dissolved Li2Sx species migrate between the cathode and anode, causing the "shuttle effect," which severely degrades the cycle life [6].
To address this, Takahashi et al. demonstrated that confining sulfur within microporous carbon (pore diameter < 2 nm) can suppress the shuttle effect [5].
In such systems, the micropores are smaller than the solvated Li ions, preventing solvent interaction with the Li2Sx species and thereby inhibiting their leaching into the electrolyte.
However, the limited pore volume of microporous carbon inherently restricts the sulfur loading, reducing the overall energy density.
Alternatively, electrolyte engineering has been explored to suppress * Corresponding author.

Li2Sx dissolution.
Additives such as lithium nitrate (LiNO3) are known to mitigate the shuttle effect [8–10].

LiNO3 decomposes on the cathode surface to form various non-stoichiometric decomposition products (e. g., LixNOy), which act as oxidation catalysts to convert dissolved Li2Sx back to elemental sulfur during charging, thereby suppressing the shuttle reaction [9].
Torii et al. reported that fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC)-based electrolytes impede Li2Sx dissolution through the formation of a stable protective layer derived from FEC decomposition [11].
This passivation layer remains stable during subsequent cycles, enabling reversible Li-S reactions without the need for LiNO3.
Consequently, FEC-based Li-S batteries can operate over a wide voltage window without significant polysulfide leaching.
Beyond these surface passiv­ ation strategies, recent advancements have also explored modifying the intrinsic Li+ solvation structure to suppress the shuttle effect.

For instance, high-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) [12,13] and localized high-concentration electrolytes (LHCEs) [14,15] have been widely investigated, as they inherently restrict polysulfide solubility by mini­ mizing the amount of free solvent molecules.
Despite these successes in suppressing polysulfide dissolution, a critical factor determining the practical energy density of Li-S batteries is the electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratio [16].

While a low E/S ratio is essential for achieving high energy density, Li-S batteries typically consume more electrolyte through irreversible side reactions compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries, leading to a shortened cycle life under lean-electrolyte conditions [16–18].

Furthermore, carbonate-based solvents like FEC, as well as the massive amounts of heavy lithium salts used in HCEs and LHCEs, possess high densities, which increases the total weight of the cell and lowers the gravimetric energy density.
In contrast, ether-based electrolytes have lower den­ sities, facilitating a reduced E/S ratio and higher energy density.
How­ ever, as previously noted, ether-based systems suffer from poor cycle life due to severe Li2Sx dissolution.
Therefore, it is imperative to develop an electrolyte that combines low density with the ability to suppress pol­ ysulfide dissolution to achieve both high energy density and long-term stability.

In this study, we focus on a novel fluoroether, 1,1,1-trifluoro-2- (2- methoxyethoxy)ethane (C14), designed by introducing an electronwithdrawing trifluoromethyl (-CF3) group into the terminal of a con­ ventional dimethoxyethane (DME) skeleton.

It is noteworthy that C14 possesses a relatively low density of 1.16 g cm−3, which is lower than those of other typical shuttle-suppressing solvents such as FEC (~1.32 g cm−3) and sulfolane (~1.26 g cm−3).
To fundamentally suppress the shuttle effect without relying on high salt concentrations, weakly solvating solvents have garnered significant attention.
However, conventional designs face a severe practical tradeoff.

While recently reported weakly solvating fluoroethers (WSEs) can suppress polysulfide dissolution, they often rely on specific salts such as LiFSI [19], which is generally considered less compatible with Li-S systems due to potential side reactions with polysulfides.
Alterna­ tively, low-molecular-weight mono-ethers (e.g., dipropyl ether or methyl tert‐butyl ether) that exhibit weakly solvating properties suffer from excessively low boiling points [20].
Such high volatility makes them incompatible with standard battery manufacturing processes, particularly the vacuum electrolyte injection step.
C14 was conceptually designed to overcome this structural dilemma.

By integrating a single -CF3 group exclusively at the terminal of the highly flexible DME back­ bone, C14 strategically balances three critical requirements within a single molecule: (1) sufficient solvating power to dissolve 1.0 M LiTFSI, (2) the delocalization of molecular surface charge to suppress poly­ sulfide ionization, and (3) a practically viable boiling point of 104 ◦C, which enables stable vacuum filling procedures.

We investigate the electrochemical properties of Li-S batteries using C14-based electrolytes and evaluate their effectiveness in suppressing Li2Sx dissolution while maintaining a relatively low-density compared to alternative functional electrolytes profile. 2.
Preparation of active materials The cathode active material was a carbon-sulfur (C-S) composite prepared by encapsulating sulfur into mesoporous carbon.

Sulfur pow­ der (sulfur sublimed, FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp., Osaka, Japan) and mesoporous carbon (Cnovel®, Toyo Tanso Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan) with an average pore diameter of 5 nm were mixed in a weight ratio of 65:35 (Sulfur:Carbon).
The mixture was sealed in a vessel and heated at 155 ◦C for 6 h to obtain the C-S composite, following the method described by Takahashi et al.
The morphology and pore distribution of the pristine mesoporous Cnovel®, as well as the thermal properties of the synthesized C-S composite, are presented in Figure S1 (a-c). 2.2.

Morphological and elemental characterization The surface morphology of the prepared C-S composite was observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Flex SEM 1000, Hitachi High- Tech Corp., Tokyo, Japan).
To investigate morphological changes dur­ ing cycling, the cathode and anode were harvested from the cell and analyzed via SEM.
Elemental distribution within the C-S composite and the harvested electrodes was visualized using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).
Furthermore, the fine structure of the C-S com­ posite was characterized using field-emission scanning electron micro­ scopy (FE-SEM, SU-9000, Hitachi High-Tech Corp., Tokyo, Japan).
To accurately determine the surface composition distribution of the C-S composite, EDX analysis was performed at a low accelerating voltage of 5 kV. 2.3.
Electrolyte preparation Two electrolytes were prepared for this study.

The baseline electro­ lyte (denoted as ELDD) consisted of 1.0 M lithium bis(tri­ fluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, Kishida Chemical Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan) dissolved in a binary solvent mixture of 1,2-dimethoxy­ ethane (DME, FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp., Saitama, Japan) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL, FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp., Saitama, Japan) (1:1 v/v).
The novel electrolyte (denoted as ELC14) consisted of 1.0 M LiTFSI dissolved in 1,1,1-trifluoro-2- (2-methoxyethoxy) ethane (C14, DAIKIN INDUSTRIES, Ltd., Osaka, Japan).

The physicochemical properties of the prepared electrolytes, including viscosity, ionic con­ ductivity, lithium-ion transference number (tLi +) and density at room temperature, are summarized in Table S1 in the Supporting Information. 2.4.

Measurement of Li+ transference number The tLi + of the electrolytes was determined by measuring the selfdiffusion coefficients of the lithium cations (DLi +) and the TFSI− anions (DTFSI - ) using pulsed-field gradient nuclear magnetic resonance (PFG- NMR) spectroscopy.
The measurements were performed on a benchtop NMR spectrometer (X-Pulse, Oxford Instruments).
The tLi + was calculated based on the ratio of the diffusion coefficient of Li+ to the sum of the diffusion coefficients of the cation and anion (tLi + = DLi + / (DLi + + DTFSI - ) [21]. 2.5.

Electrochemical measurements The cathode slurry was prepared by mixing the C-S composite, acetylene black (AB, Denka Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) as a conductive additive, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC, DKS Co., Ltd., Kyoto, Japan), and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR, JSR Corp., Tokyo, Japan) in a weight ratio of 90:5:3:2.
The mixture was dispersed in deionized water to form a homogeneous paste.
This paste was cast onto aluminum foil to serve as the cathode.
After the slurry was coated onto the current D.

collector, the electrodes were dried at 60 ◦C under reduced pressure for 12 h.

This drying temperature was carefully selected to ensure the complete removal of residual moisture from the aqueous binder (CMC/ SBR) while strictly preventing the unintended volatilization of elemental sulfur, which can occur at higher temperatures under vacuum.
The sulfur loading of the cathode was 1.15 mg cm−2, and the electrode area was 1.13 cm2.

To strictly isolate and evaluate the intrinsic ability of the C14 solvent to chemically suppress polysulfide dissolution, the electro­ chemical tests were intentionally conducted under flooded conditions with an excess amount of electrolyte.
The specific current density was calculated based on the theoretical capacity of sulfur (1C = 1672 mA g- 1).

This approach ensures that the observed suppression of the shuttle effect originates fundamentally from the weakly solvating nature of the C14 molecular design, rather than from physical limitations imposed by solvent starvation (i.e., a lean E/S ratio).
The detailed morphological and compositional characterizations of the synthesized C-S composite, including SEM and EDX analyses, are provided in the Supporting In­ formation (Figure S2).

Two-electrode half-cells were assembled using the prepared cathode as the working electrode, lithium foil as the counter electrode, and a polyolefin microporous membrane as the separator, filled with the respective electrolytes. 2.6.
Analysis of solvation structure To elucidate the solvation structure of Li+ in the electrolytes, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) and Raman spectroscopy were employed.
FT-IR spectra were recorded using an ALPHA2 spectrometer (Bruker Co., Ltd., MA, USA) equipped with an attenuated total reflection (ATR) accessory.
Raman spectra were obtained using a Nanofinder 30® (Tokyo Instruments, Inc., Tokyo, Japan).
To investigate the coordination structure of polysulfides in the sol­ vents, lithium polysulfide solutions were prepared.
Li2S and elemental sulfur were mixed in a 1:7 molar ratio in 30 mL of DME or C14 and stirred for 24 h.
The resulting solutions, denoted as Li2Sx/DME and Li2Sx/C14, were analyzed via FT-IR. 2.7.
Computational details Quantum chemical calculations were performed to estimate the solvation structure of Li+ and the thermodynamic interactions between the solvents and polysulfides.
The Conductor-like Screening Model for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) method was applied using the COSMO-RS module (MOLSIS Inc., Tokyo, Japan) [22,23].

It should be noted that direct geometry optimizations of long-chain polysulfide complexes (e.g., Li2S8 with C14) for conventional binding energy calculations were computationally unfeasible, as the initial structures severely diverged and failed to form stable coordination complexes in the simulated environments.

Therefore, the probability distribution of the surface charge density, known as the σ-profile (P(σ)), was utilized as an alternative, robust thermodynamic descriptor to evaluate the interaction potential based on the intrinsic molecular charge distributions, bypassing the convergence issues associated with direct cluster optimization.
In the COSMO-RS approach, the molecular state in solution is approximated using a conductor screening model to determine the stereostructure and surface charge density (σ).
The molecular surface is divided into segments, and the interaction energy is calculated assuming contact between these segments.
The σ-profile was derived by integrating the surface segment areas having a specific charge density σ.
The coordination structure of the solvent around Li+ was estimated based on the obtained σ-profiles and interaction energies. 2.8.

Mechanism analysis To clarify the charge-discharge reaction mechanism in the Li-S bat­ teries using the fluorinated ether solvent, the surface compositions of the sulfur cathode and lithium anode at various states of charge (SOC) were analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI Quantes, ULVAC-PHI Inc., Kanagawa, Japan).
Depth profiling was performed during XPS measurements using an argon gas cluster ion beam (GCIB) to minimize etching damage.
The binding energies were calibrated refer­ encing the C–H bond peak in the C 1 s spectrum at 284.8 eV.
Furthermore, the relationship between the SOC of the sulfur cathode and its electronic structure was investigated using X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS).
Measurements were conducted at BL-11 of the Ritsu­ meikan University Synchrotron Radiation Center (Japan) using a variable-line-spacing plane grating monochromator.
Data were collected in both partial fluorescence yield (PFY) and total electron yield (TEY) modes.
For post-mortem analyses such as SEM, XPS, and XANES, the cycled cells were disassembled in an Ar-filled glovebox.

The elec­ trodes were thoroughly rinsed with dimethyl carbonate (DMC) and then dried at room temperature under reduced pressure for 12 h to remove any volatile residual solvents and electrolyte salts.
The obtained X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra were analyzed using the Athena software package [24]. 3.
Results and discussion 3.1.

Solvation structure in C14-based electrolytes To elucidate the solvation structures of Li+ ions in the ELC14 and ELDD electrolytes, FT-IR and Raman spectroscopy measurements were performed on LiTFSI/C14 and LiTFSI/DME solutions with varying salt concentrations.
Fig. 1(a) and 1(b) show the IR spectra of LiTFSI/DME and LiTFSI/ C14 solutions with concentrations of 0, 0.5, and 1.0 mol l−1.
In the spectrum of pure DME (Fig. 1(a)), a peak at roughly 1100 cm−1, corre­ sponding to the C–O-C asymmetric stretching vibration, was observed.
Upon adding LiTFSI (0.5 and 1.0 mol l−1), the intensity of this peak decreased, while new peaks appeared at approximately 1080 and 1140 cm−1.
These new peaks, which are absent in pure DME, are attributed to DME molecules coordinated to Li+.
This suggests that the bonding state of the C–O-C group changes upon coordination.

Furthermore, in the LiTFSI/DME spectra, a peak attributed to C–H bending vibrations appeared at roughly 870 cm−1, while the peak intensity at roughly 850 cm−1 decreased as the LiTFSI concentration increased.
It has been re­ ported that the spectral shape in this region depends on the conforma­ tion of the diether structure [25,26].
The variations in peak intensities at 870, 850, and 820 cm−1 with solution concentration suggest that DME undergoes a conformational change upon coordinating with Li+.
Fig. 1(b) presents the IR spectra of the LiTFSI/C14 solutions.
A peak at approximately 1070 cm−1 was observed to increase in intensity with increasing electrolyte concentration.
This peak is attributed to the S-N-S group contained in the LiTFSI electrolyte salt [27].

Furthermore, similar to the DME system, the peak at roughly 1100 cm−1 (C–O-C asymmetric stretching) decreased in intensity as the solution concentration increased, suggesting that the C–O-C structure in C14 coordinates to Li+.
However, unlike DME, the spectral shape in the 850–870 cm−1 region remained almost unchanged regardless of the solution concentration.
This result suggests that the conformation of C14 does not change significantly when coordinating to Li+ [28].
From these results, it is considered that while C14 has a solvation structure similar to DME, its coordination geometry with Li+ differs from that of DME.
Fig. 1(c) shows the Raman spectra of DME and LiTFSI/DME solu­ tions.
The peak intensity at roughly 870 cm−1 increased with increasing solution concentration.

Although a similar trend was confirmed in the IR spectra, the relationship between electrolyte concentration and peak intensity was found to be much clearer in the Raman spectra than in the IR spectra.
These concentration-dependent changes in peak intensity likely arise from conformational changes rather than shifts in polarity [29].
Fig. 1(d) shows the Raman spectra of C14 and LiTFSI/C14 solutions.

The intensity of the shoulder at roughly 870 cm−1 increased slightly with increasing concentration.

A similar trend was observed in the LiTFSI/ DME Raman spectra; however, the increase in shoulder intensity relative to the increase in electrolyte concentration was smaller in the LiTFSI/ C14 solution than in the LiTFSI/DME solution.
This suggests that C14 is less likely to form a gauche solvation structure compared to DME.

plateau was observed at approximately 2.3 V during the charging pro­ cess, which did not terminate.
This infinite charging behavior is attrib­ uted to the shuttle effect, caused by the migration of Li2Sx formed during charging to the anode surface [30].
On the other hand, the Li-SELC14 cell (Fig. 2(b)) exhibited reversible charge-discharge profiles without such a plateau.
The high reversibility observed in Li-SELC14 suggests that the dissolution of Li2Sx is effectively suppressed.

The mechanism of Li2Sx dissolution has been reported to involve the coordination of solvent molecules to Li+ within the Li2Sx structure, which induces ionization and leaching into the electrolyte [31,32].
Specif­ ically, DME coordinates with Li+ by adopting tgt, tgg, and tgg’ confor­ mations, thereby facilitating the dissociation of Li2Sx.
However, as suggested by the spectroscopic results in Section 3.1, C14 has a lower tendency to coordinate with Li+.
Consequently, it is inferred that C14 is sterically or electronically hindered from coordinating with Li2Sx, which prevents the dissolution of polysulfides into the electrolyte.
Finally, considering the practical energy density discussed in the Introduction, the density of the electrolyte and the achievable E/S ratio are critical parameters.
The measured densities of the prepared electrolytes are summarized in Table S1.

While the density of ELC14 is higher than that of the conventional DME-based ELDD, it remains lower than those of other typical shuttle-suppressing systems such as carbonate-based electrolytes or HCEs.
Furthermore, the fundamental suppression of polysulfide dissolution demonstrated in this study addresses the primary cause of continuous electrolyte consumption.
Theoretically, minimizing these irreversible side reactions is a prerequisite for reducing the required electrolyte volume in practical cells.

Therefore, the C14-based electrolyte provides a promising conceptual pathway toward achieving high-energy-density Li-S batteries by combining a relatively low-density profile with the inherent capability to suppress polysulfide leaching without relying on excessively high salt concentrations.
The shift in the discharge plateau potentials between the two electrolytes indicates a fundamental difference in the reaction intermediates due to the distinct solvation capabilities of the solvents.
To further investigate the elec­ trochemical reaction processes, the corresponding dQ/dV profiles are provided in the Supporting Information (Figure S3).
The dQ/dV profile of the ELDD cell exhibits broad and relatively fluctuating reduction peaks.

This profile suggests that the dissolution of polysulfides leads to the coexistence of multiple intermediate states in the vicinity of the electrode, resulting in a complex overlap of electrochemical reactions.
Conversely, the ELC14 cell displays noticeably sharper peaks.

This characteristic indicates that the effective suppression of polysulfide dissolution in the weakly solvating C14 prevents such complexity, allowing a more uniform, single electrochemical reaction to proceed at the specific reaction potential.

To further evaluate the practical aspects of the weakly solvating concept, the cycle performance, Coulombic ef­ ficiency (calculated as charge capacity divided by discharge capacity), and rate capability of the ELC14 cell are summarized in Figure S3(a).
It should be noted that the conventional ELDD cell suffers from a severe continuous shuttle effect under these testing conditions, making it difficult to maintain normal reversible cycling.

In contrast, the ELC14 cell successfully completes the charging process and enables continuous cycling, demonstrating that the intrinsic weakly solvating nature of C14 effectively suppresses polysulfide dissolution.

It is noteworthy that the C14-based electrolyte possesses an ionic conductivity (0.111 S m−1) that is more than one order of magnitude lower than that of the conventional DME-based electrolyte (1.277 S m−1), alongside a higher viscosity (Table S1).
Generally, such sluggish ion transport properties would severely restrict the rate performance of the cell.
However, despite these apparent transport bottlenecks, the ELC14 cell exhibits a relatively high rate capability, maintaining sig­ nificant reversible capacity even at elevated C-rates (Figure S3).
This unexpectedly favorable rate performance can be attributed to the remarkably high tLi + of 0.599 determined via PFG-NMR.
In conventional DME-based systems, tLi + values typically range from 0.2 to 0.4 due to strong chelation [33,34].
A high transference number effectively mitigates the development of severe salt concentration gradients (con­ centration polarization) near the electrode surface during high-current operation.

Therefore, the highly efficient cation transport (high tLi +) in the weakly solvating C14 system successfully compensates for its low absolute ionic conductivity, enabling uniform redox reactions and sus­ taining electrochemical activity under increased current densities.
Over 50 cycles, a gradual capacity fade is observed, and the Coulombic effi­ ciency stabilizes at approximately 106%.

The Coulombic efficiency exceeding 100% indicates that the charge capacity is slightly larger than the discharge capacity, suggesting the presence of minor parasitic reactions-such as a slight residual shuttle effect or oxidative decompo­ sition of the electrolyte-during the charging process.
Furthermore, the strong thermodynamic confinement of polysulfides in C14 forces the redox reaction into a sluggish, undissolved solid-state conversion.
The observed capacity decay is likely a consequence of these kinetic limi­ tations of the un-dissolved intermediates combined with the continuous minor side reactions.
Further cell engineering to address these kinetic and interfacial challenges represents an important direction for future research. 3.3.

Coordination structure of solvents with Li2Sx Fig. 3(a) displays photographs of the Li2Sx/DME and Li2Sx/C14 mixtures prepared to investigate the solvation interaction between the solvents and lithium polysulfides.
The Li2Sx/DME mixture was observed to be a transparent, reddish-brown solution.
This distinct coloration is attributed to the formation of soluble polysulfide species solvated by DME, indicating high solubility.
In contrast, the Li2Sx/C14 mixture appeared as a yellow suspension, suggesting that Li2Sx is sparingly sol­ uble in the C14 solvent.
To further elucidate the structural changes of the solvents in these mixtures, FT-IR spectra were recorded, as shown in Figs. 3(b) and 3(c).

As shown in Fig. 3(b), in the IR spectra of Li2Sx/DME, the intensity of the peak at approximately 1100 cm−1 decreased with increasing Li2Sx con­ centration, while the shoulder peak at approximately 1080 cm−1 inten­ sified.
The peak at ~1100 cm−1 is assigned to the C–O-C asymmetric stretching of free DME, whereas the peak at ~1080 cm−1 is attributed to the C–O-C stretching of DME coordinated to Li+.
These spectral changes indicate that the ether oxygen atoms of DME actively coordinate to the lithium ions in the polysulfides, facilitating their dissolution.
Conversely, the IR spectra of Li2Sx/C14 (Fig. 3(c)) exhibited virtually identical profiles regardless of the Li2Sx concentration.
The absence of significant spectral shifts or intensity changes in the C–O-C stretching region implies that C14 has a significantly lower tendency to coordinate with Li2Sx compared to DME.
This lack of coordination prevents the solvation and subsequent dissolution of polysulfides, consistent with the visual observation of the suspension. 3.4.

Computational analysis of Li-solvent interaction via COSMO-RS The experimental results from the FT-IR analysis of Li2Sx solutions revealed a distinct difference in the solubility of Li2Sx depending on the solvent species.
We hypothesized that this disparity stems from the difference in the interaction strength between the solvent molecules and the Li+ ions within the Li2Sx structure.
To verify this hypothesis, the surface charge density distributions of DME and C14 were calculated using the COSMO-RS method.

Fig. 4(a) presents the calculated σ-profiles (probability distribution of surface charge density), while Fig. 4(b) and 4(c) visualize the surface charge density distributions on the molecular surfaces of DME and C14, respectively.
As shown in the σ-profiles (Fig. 4(a)), DME exhibits a broader dis­ tribution in the region of high charge density (σ ≥0.01 e Å−2) compared to C14.
In the molecular surface visualizations (Fig. 4(b) and 4(c)), the red-colored regions correspond to these areas of high surface charge density (σ ≥0.01).

For DME (Fig. 4(b)), it was observed that the charge density on the surfaces of the two oxygen atoms is significantly higher than that on other atoms.
Similarly, C14 (Fig. 4(c)) also exhibits high charge density on its oxygen atoms.
However, the total surface area corresponding to these high charge density regions is notably smaller in C14 compared to DME.
This reduction is attributed to the electron-withdrawing effect of the trifluoromethyl group (-CF3), which causes the delocalization of surface charge across the C14 molecule.

Based on these findings, the reduced solvation capability of C14 to­ ward Li2Sx compared to DME is ascribed to two primary factors: (1) the difficulty in adopting the cis-conformation due to the steric hindrance of the -CF3 group (as discussed in Section 3.1), and (2) the delocalization of molecular surface charge induced by the electron-withdrawing -CF3 group.
These characteristics suggest that employing C14 as a solvent for Li-S battery electrolytes is an effective strategy to suppress Li2Sx disso­ lution and mitigate the shuttle effect. 3.5.

Ex-situ morphological analysis during cycling To elucidate the differences in the charge-discharge reaction mech­ anisms between the Li-SELDD and Li-SELC14 systems, ex-situ FE-SEM observations were performed on cathodes harvested at various states of charge (SOC).
The sampling points are indicated by square (■) and triangular (▴) symbols in the charge-discharge profiles shown in Fig. 5 (a) and 5(b).
FE-SEM images of the pristine C-S cathode are shown in Fig. 5(c) (corresponding to points ■1 and ▴1).

At 15% depth of discharge (DOD) (Points ■2 and ▴2), the surface morphologies of the cathodes in both Li-SELDD (Fig. 5(c)) and Li- SELC14 (Fig. 5(h)) appeared similar to that of the pristine electrode.
However, at 50% DOD, a distinct difference emerged.
Particulate pre­ cipitates with a diameter of approximately 50 nm were formed on the surface of the Li-SELDD cathode (Point ■3, Fig. 5(d)).
EDX analysis detected high concentrations of sulfur and oxygen from these pre­ cipitates (Figure S4), suggesting they are decomposition products of the LiTFSI electrolyte salt.

In contrast, the surface of the Li-SELC14 cathode at 50% DOD (Point ▴3, Fig. 5(i)) remained comparable to the pristine state, indicating superior interfacial stability against electrolyte decomposition.
At 100% DOD (Points ■4 and ▴4), the surfaces of both cathodes (Fig. 5(e) and 5(j)) were covered with precipitates.
EDX analysis of the Li-SELDD surface revealed an oxygen- and sulfur-rich composition with reduced carbon signal compared to the 50% DOD state.
This indicates the formation of discharge products, likely Li2Sx and Li2S.
Interestingly, for Li-SELC14, while the precipitate-covered regions were rich in sulfur and oxygen, the exposed regions showed higher carbon signals (Figure S4).
During the subsequent charging process, at 50% SOC (Points ■5 and ▴5), the precipitates observed after discharge disappeared from the surfaces of both electrodes (Fig. 5(f) and 5(k)).
This disappearance in­ dicates the oxidation of solid discharge products into soluble species or elemental sulfur.
Finally, at 100% SOC (Points ■6 and ▴6), the surface morphologies of both electrodes (Fig. 5(g) and 5(l)) reverted to a state similar to the pristine electrode.

However, semi-quantitative EDX analysis revealed that the peak intensity ratio of sulfur to carbon (S/C) on the Li-SELC14 cathode was significantly higher than that on the Li- SELDD cathode (Figure S5).
This higher sulfur retention implies that the elution of long-chain Li2Sx formed during the latter stages of charging was effectively suppressed by the C14 solvent. 3.6.

Fig. 6(c) and 6(d) display the S 2p XPS spectra corresponding to the indicated DOD/SOC points.
In the pristine electrode, peaks attributed to S were observed at approximately 163 and 164.5 eV.

For the Li-SELDD system, as the DOD increased (Points ■2 to ■4), the intensity of S peaks decreased, while peaks at 160 and 161.5 eV attributed to Li2S and Li2Sx increased, corresponding to the progression of the discharge reaction (Eq. 1).
However, at 100% DOD (Point ■4), peaks corresponding to Li2Sx were still observable, indicating the presence of unreacted in­ termediates [35].
This incomplete conversion likely accounts for the lower specific capacity (~1200 mAh g−1) compared to the theoretical value.
During the charging process, although the Li2S peaks decreased, peaks assigned to unreacted Li2S and Li2Sx persisted even after charging to 2000 mAh g−1 (Point ■6).
This incomplete oxidation is attributed to the shuttle effect, where continuous polysulfide migration prevents the completion of the charging reaction.
Conversely, in the Li-SELC14 system, the S 2p spectrum at 50% SOC (Point ▴5) showed a significantly higher intensity for elemental S compared to the Li-SELDD system (Point ■5).
Furthermore, the spec­ trum at 100% SOC (Point ▴6) closely resembled that of the 15% DOD state (Point ▴2), demonstrating high reversibility.
These results suggest that the shuttle effect is effectively suppressed in the C14 electrolyte, enabling the efficient recovery of active sulfur during the charge cycle.

This remarkable difference at the anode interface conclusively proves that the intrinsic weakly solvating capability of the C14 solvent effectively confines the polysulfides within the cathode region, successfully pre­ venting their parasitic crossover and deposition on the lithium metal surface.
Fig. 7(a-d) present the S K-edge XANES spectra obtained via TEY and PFY.
Guo et al. predicted the XANES spectra based on the composition and structure of Li2Sx using Density Functional Theory (DFT) calcula­ tions [36–39].
Based on these theoretical results, the spectral peaks observed in this study were assigned as follows.
For Li-SELDD (Fig. 7(a) and 7(b)), a peak assigned to Li2S4 (~2482 eV) appeared at 15% DOD and subsequently decreased, while the Li2S2 peak (~2478.2 eV) increased.
Notably, at 50% and 100% DOD, a preedge feature appeared at 2470.3 eV.
To accurately interpret this feature, it is crucial to note that our XANES measurements were per­ formed on the undissolved solid cathode.

According to theoretical and experimental XANES studies [33,40–42], this pre-edge feature origi­ nates from the creation of unoccupied orbitals on sulfur atoms when Li+ ions are dissociated or extracted.

In the ELDD system, the strong coor­ dinating ability of DME heavily solvates the Li+ ions, which is thought to effectively extract them from the solid Li2S4 on the cathode, creating Li-site vacancies (defects).

Consequently, the remaining solid poly­ sulfides with these Li-defects are considered to exhibit an electronic state analogous to that of solvated polysulfides in the liquid phase, where the disruption of local coordination generates unoccupied orbitals on the sulfur atoms, manifesting as the pre-edge peak at 2470.3 eV.
Addition­ ally, the absorption edge attributed to S8 at 2471.8 eV was confirmed even in the DOD 100% spectrum, indicating incomplete reduction.
Furthermore, the intensity of the pre-edge at 2470.3 eV was higher at 100% DOD compared to 50% DOD.
This result suggests that the number of defects in Li2S4 contained in the cathode at 100% DOD increased compared to that at 50% DOD.
During charging, Li2S4 re-formed but persisted even at the end of charge, further confirming the shuttle effect.

In contrast, for the Li-SELC14 system (Fig. 7(c) and (d)), during the discharge process from 50% to 100% DOD, the intensities of peaks assigned to Li2S4 and Li2S3 decreased, while those assigned to Li2S2 and Li2S increased.
During the subsequent charging process from 100% DOD to 50% SOC, the peak intensities for Li2S and Li2S3 decreased, whereas the peak for Li2S2 increased.
From 50% SOC to the end of charge, the peaks assigned to Li2S2, Li2S3, and Li2S4 decreased, and the intensity of the peak assigned to S8 increased.
The spectral shape at the end of charge was confirmed to be similar to that at 15% DOD.
Notably, the pre-edge feature at 2470.3 eV was absent in the Li- SELC14 spectra throughout the charge-discharge process.
This absence strongly suggests that the weakly solvating C14 solvent does not strongly interact with the Li+ ions in the polysulfides.
Thus, it is considered that C14 cannot extract Li+ to create vacancies, effectively maintaining the polysulfides in an undissolved solid state without generating such unoccupied sulfur orbitals.

This finding is consistent with the COSMO-RS and IR results discussed previously, which showed that the delocalized surface charge and steric hindrance of C14 prevent effective coordination with Li2Sx.
Additionally, in both systems, the ratio of Li2Sx peaks to S8 peaks was lower in the PFY spectra compared to the TEY spectra.
This discrepancy suggests that unreacted sulfur remains in the bulk (several μm depth) of the C-S particles even when the surface has reacted.

It implies that the electrochemical reaction proceeds more readily at the particle surface than in the bulk, which explains why the practical specific capacities of Li-SELDD (1200 mAh g−1) and Li-SELC14 (1000 mAh g−1) are lower than the theoretical maximum (1672 mAh g−1).

attributed to the suppression of Li2Sx dissolution by the C14 solvent.
Mechanistic investigations using COSMO-RS calculations revealed that the surface charge density of the C14 molecule is significantly more delocalized compared to that of DME.
Based on this finding, we hy­ pothesized that solvents with low, delocalized surface charge density, such as C14, inhibit the ionization of Li2Sx and its subsequent leaching into the electrolyte.
To validate this hypothesis, the evolution of the electronic structure of the sulfur cathode during the charge-discharge process was probed via XAS.
In the Li-SELDD system, a pre-edge feature at 2470.3 eV, assigned to lithium defects in the polysulfide structure, was observed in the S K-edge XANES spectra at DODs of 50% and greater.
These defects are interpreted as the result of Li2Sx ionization induced by the strong coordination of the solvent.

In stark contrast, this pre-edge feature was notably absent in the Li-SELC14 spectra at all depths of discharge, indicating that the ionization of Li2Sx is effectively suppressed in the C14 environment.

In conclusion, the C14 solvent effectively mitigates the ionization and dissolution of Li2Sx due to its delocalized surface charge and steric properties, thereby enabling the stable and reversible operation of Li-S batteries.

More broadly, this work highlights that molecular design focusing on charge delocalization in fluorinated ethers serves as a highly effective and generalizable strategy for developing advanced electro­ lytes in next-generation Li-S batteries.

The composite particles were observed to have a diameter of approximately 2 μm, exhibiting a surface morphology nearly identical to that of the pristine Cnovel carbon.
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) of the C-S composite revealed a weight loss of approximately 65 wt% when heated to 500 °C under an inert atmosphere.
This weight loss corresponds to the sublimation of sulfur.

The absence of bulk sulfur agglomerates on the particle surface in the SEM images, combined with the significant sulfur content confirmed by TGA, suggests that the sulfur is effectively infused within the internal mesoporous structure of the Cnovel matrix rather than accumulating on the exterior surface.
To further verify the distribution of sulfur, elemental mapping was performed using EDX, as shown in Figure S2(b).
The mapping reveals that the spatial distribution of sulfur (S) coincides well with that of carbon (C), indicating that both elements are present in the same regions.
This result confirms the successful formation of a composite where sulfur is homogeneously composited with the Cnovel framework.
